items.title: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026
items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026 Zillow forecasts 3.0% rent inflation, 3.6% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on November 17, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to firm into the end of the year. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 around 3.0% and OER near 3.5%. Part of the year-end rise is mechanical, as the BLS folded October 2025's increase ,missed during the government shutdown, into April 2026. This adjustment will add about 0.3 points to the true underlying annual rate until April 2027. From last month's forecast, the year-end outlook was revised up for OER (3.44% to 3.53%) and down for rent (3.06% to 3.04%). New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, no longer pulling down housing inflation measures. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. items.title: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook
items.description: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook Written by Kenny Lee on November 18, 2026 What happened Housing starts jumped 9.9% from September to 1.309 million SAAR in October, up 2.8% from September last year. While starts in the West fell to the lowest in more than six years, the Midwest and South showed strength, rising 48.4% and 10.5%, respectively. However, sharp declines in new-construction permits indicate builders’ caution. Authorized units declined 7.4% to 1.295 million in October, with the single-family segment down sharply by 8.7%. All four Census regions saw declines in single-family construction permits. While notoriously volatile, multifamily housing starts nationwide jumped 25.5% to 433 thousand units in October. Although multifamily permits fell 5.2% from September to 475 thousand units in October, the latest pace is an improvement from this summer. Compared to last year, the three-month moving average of multifamily permits was up 3.5% from a year ago. Why it matters Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October , the largest year-over-year drop since 2023. Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes , the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane. The flipside of cooling buyer demand is skyrocketing renter demand. As elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead, renter demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Although the industry has been grappling with high new construction inventory over the past few years since the construction boom in 2022 and 2023, recent Zillow data shows market fundamentals started improving this year. The typical multifamily rent increased 2.5% year over year in October, compared to 1.3% growth one year ago, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Stronger rent growth reflects a resurgence of renter demand across the country. Recent gains in multifamily permits could be an early sign that the supply outlook is transitioning to growth. That said, it is worth noting that the Census Bureau's multifamily construction data relies on a survey with a small sample and is often subject to large revisions, and it will take additional data to see whether the recent gains indicate a new trend. Although developers still face challenging market conditions, such as high costs of construction financing, building materials, and skilled labor, a sustained improvement in multifamily supply will help alleviate the pressure on renters. items.title: Pending Home Sales Fall in October As Rates Hit 2026 Peak
items.description: Pending Home Sales Fall in October As Rates Hit 2026 Peak By Hannah Jones Nov 18, 2026 What did pending home sales look like in October? Pending home sales fell to another record-low, easing 4.7% in October, as mortgage rates hit a recent peak of 7.4%, and were down 16.7% from a year earlier. Rates have since eased back into the low 7% range, but October’s hot inflation data , released last week, is likely to push them higher again. Headline inflation rose 0.4% month over month, well above the 0.2% to 0.3% forecast, and core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. Markets now expect that a Fed rate hike is coming in December. Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued. What does this mean for buyers, sellers, and the housing market? All four regions saw declines both month over month and year over year, led by the West, where contract signings fell 6.9% for the month and 20.3% from a year earlier. The South followed with declines of 6.3% and 18.7%, then the Midwest with 2.7% and 14.0%. The Northeast had the smallest monthly drop, 0.8%, but was still down 11.1% from a year earlier. Even though all four regions saw dramatic cooling, the relative strength of the Midwest and Northeast are clear, due largely to still-scarce inventory conditions. Though all large metros saw pending home sales ease annually, the smallest drops were in Cincinnati (-4.7%), Austin (-9.7%) and Hartford, CT (-10.0%). Did the run-up to the November midterms keep buyers on the sidelines? Possibly. Some home shoppers may have held off to wait for the results, but rising rates are the more likely culprit . Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment. That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb. Affordability remains the limiting factor in today’s housing market. The typical mortgage-holder would see a $1,100 increase in their monthly payment if they bought a median-priced home today. Sellers have shown some flexibility, with lower asking prices and more price cuts , but buyers have not responded with much enthusiasm at these rates. Sellers are only willing to come down so far and buyers are only willing to stretch so far, and a gap still separates the two. As a result, transaction volume in October hit its lowest level in 16 years . There is an upside for buyers who can afford to act. With fewer shoppers in the market, they will face less competition for each listing, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more willing to negotiate on price, repairs, or closing costs.

items.title: Mortgage Rates Climb Again, and Spring Could Still See Rates Above 7%
items.description: Mortgage Rates Climb Again, and Spring Could Still See Rates Above 7% Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. Written by Kara Ng on November 18, 2026 In short: Mortgage rates rose again after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report reinforced expectations for a December Fed hike. With new-lease rent growth picking up, shelter may offer the Fed less help in bringing inflation down in 2027. Mortgage rates turn higher after a hot October inflation report After a few weeks of easing from the recent peak, mortgage rates rose again. One contributor was the hot October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, which cemented a December Fed rate increase and highlighted the possibility of a 50bp hike (roughly at 10% probability , as of November 18). Shelter was a major driver of October inflation, and Zillow expects housing inflation to keep firming . New-lease rents are growing at their fastest pace in 2025-2026, so they’re no longer pulling down housing inflation measures, and forecasts for on-market rents have been revised upward in recent months. In other words, while oil-related developments could ease some inflation pressure, firmer rent growth means the Fed may get less help from shelter in 2027. What’s the impact on housing? Pending sales fell sharply in October , as both the level of mortgage rates and the speed at which they rose led buyers to step back. Because pending sales are a leading indicator of closed sales, October’s drop means closed sales should be weaker this month. Zillow’s forecast for 2027 calls for mortgage rates to stay above 7% until around mid-year, with sales falling 3.5%. However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner. With inventory forecast to rise about 11% next year, there should be enough supply to meet demand if buyers return. items.title: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report
items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 18, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share Month-Over-Month 4.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 16.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions WASHINGTON (November 18, 2026) – Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” October 2026 National Pending Home Sales 4.7% decrease month-over-month 16.7% decrease year-over-year October 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 0.8% decrease month-over-month 11.1% decrease year-over-year Midwest 2.7% decrease month-over-month 14.0% decrease year-over-year South 6.3% decrease month-over-month 18.7% decrease year-over-year West 6.9% decrease month-over-month 20.3% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Cincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, IN (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, IL-IN (-11.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-12.7%) Jacksonville, FL (-12.8%) Cleveland, OH (-12.8%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 14, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 14, 2026) By Anthony Smith Nov 19, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Mortgage rates remain in the lower 7% range, and both sides of the market continue to pull back. Active inventory is up 8.6% from a year ago. However, this is not because sellers are rushing in. New listings are still running below last year’s pace, and homes are taking 2 days longer to sell, the widest gap since mid-April. Sellers have kept cutting their asking prices, with the median listing price down 2.4% year over year, matching its steepest decline since early October, yet buyers have not returned in force. The latest contract data shows how deep the pullback runs. Pending home sales fell 4.7% in October to another record low and were down 16.7% from a year earlier, as mortgage rates peaked at 7.4%. Rates have since eased, but October’s hot inflation data has markets expecting a Fed rate hike in December, which could push borrowing costs higher again. For buyers who can afford to act, there is an upside with fewer shoppers meaning less competition, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are more open to negotiating on price, repairs, or closing costs. Active inventory climbed 8.6% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.6% compared to a year ago, the fourth straight week of growth at 8% or higher. Inventory has been building momentum since July, rising from roughly 2% year-over-year growth in mid-July to nearly 9% now. This pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers, but by a pullback in buyer activity that is letting unsold listings pile up. Year-to-date, active inventory is up 5.1%. Homes spent 2 days longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 66 days, with homes selling 2 days slower than the same time last year. This marks the fourth week in a row that time on market has slowed, and the widest gap since mid-April, after a long stretch reaching back to May of homes selling at the same pace or faster than last year. As mortgage rates stay above 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 3.5% year-over-year New listing activity fell 3.5% year over year, the seventh straight week of annual declines. That is a milder drop than last week’s 10.3%, but sellers are still staying put because buyers remain disengaged. Our latest analysis of Census data found that 59% of owner-occupied homes still carry a mortgage , and owners with low-rate loans are reluctant to give up that rate for a costlier loan on their next home, which makes relocating a less attractive proposition. Year-to-date, new listings are down 0.6%. The median listing price fell 2.4% year-over-year The median listing price was $405,000, down 2.4% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 44 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.2% year over year, and the number of listings with price cuts rose 10.5%. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch, and sellers are responding slowly. The softness is concentrated in existing homes: our latest new construction report found existing home prices 1.5% below 2025 levels in the third quarter, while new home listing prices were flat, with builders offering reduced mortgage rates to sweeten deals. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: New Construction Gives Mixed Signals in October
items.description: New Construction Gives Mixed Signals in October By Joel Berner Nov 18, 2026 October 2026 New Residential Construction What happened New residential construction sent some mixed signals in October and saw a recent trend of stronger permitting activity reverse itself. Permits fell 7.4% month over month and 8.7% year over year, while starts rose 9.9% from a weak September readout and 2.8% from their level last October. Completions themselves were mixed, rising 6.5% month over month but falling 10.4% year over year. The challenges facing builders have not subsided, and while there are some glimmers of hope in the housing starts figures, it must be noted that the current pace of single family home starts is still below last year’s actual total. This month’s data is an improvement, but from a very low baseline readout in both September and last October. Where it happened New housing units permitted for construction fell to their lowest level since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in May 2020. The pullback was most evident for single family homes, which fell 8.7% month over month and 12.9% year over year, while multifamily fell just 5.2% month over month and 0.4% year over year. Permitting was the lone bright spot in September’s new construction data release, but this month it comes as a disappointment. Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it’s rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand. This month’s data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on. Regionally, only the Midwest posted any kind of a gain in permitting, though that was concentrated in the multifamily space rather than single family. The other regions all saw a slowdown, most notably the West, which saw 20.0% fewer permits issued than it did this time last year. Housing starts had a better month in October following a very weak September. Gains in the Midwest (up 48.4% month over month and 17.2% year over year) and South (up 10.5% month over month and 12.2% year over year) offset losses in the Northeast (down 20.8% month over month and 34.5% year over year) and West (down 2.6% month over month and 11.6% year over year). Overall, multifamily projects pulled most of the weight for this improvement, rising 25.5% from September and 22.0% from last October while single family projects rose just 4.0% from September and fell 3.2% from last October. Nationwide asking rents finally broke their streak of falling for over 3 years while for-sale home listings have seen prices falling for all of 2026, so it makes sense for builders to be targeting large apartment building projects rather than single family homes. Completions improved month over month but remained below last year’s levels for both single family (up 6.3% month over month, down 10.7% year over year) and multifamily (up 9.0% month over month, down 9.0% year over year) projects. Again, it’s important to note that the current pace of completions (1,272,000 units) is still well below last year’s total (1,488,500 units), meaning that fewer new homes are coming onto the market. Regionally, the Midwest (+17.2%) and West (+3.7%) posted year-over-year gains while the Northeast (-34.5%) and South (-17.6%) saw significant pullback from last October. What does this mean for homebuyers, sellers, homeowners, and the housing market If you focus on home starts, this month’s new construction data is a welcome improvement from last month’s, but zooming out for more context shows a residential construction industry that is still struggling to find its footing. Builder confidence is at a 14-year low, and softening permits will put downward pressure on starts and completions in the months to come. In a country facing a supply gap of over four million homes, this represents a step in the wrong direction.

items.title: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER
items.description: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER Single-family leasing activity increased as rental prices edged higher HOUSTON -- (November 18, 2026) -- Houston-area renters kept the market moving in October, leasing more homes than a year ago even as rental prices edged higher. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Rental Market Update, 3,850 single-family homes were leased, a 3.5% increase from 3,720 in October 2025. A healthy supply of rental homes helped keep prices relatively stable. The average lease price for a single-family home rose just 1.2% to $2,293, compared to $2,266 in October 2025. "With affordability still top of mind, many people are taking a closer look at their housing options and what works best for their budgets," said HAR Chair-Elect Kat Robinson with SERHANT. "As we head toward the end of the year, that will continue to play a big role in whether people decide to rent or buy. For renters, it's encouraging to see that prices haven't changed much from last year." Townhomes and condominiums also saw an increase in leasing activity. A total of 638 properties were leased in October, up 9.1% from 585 a year earlier. The average lease price rose 4.0% to $1,943, while the median price increased 2.9% to $1,800. Rental inventory in this segment continued to expand. New listings increased 1.7% to 1,143 properties, while active listings rose 3.3% to 2,387. Townhomes and condominiums spent an average of 48 days on the market, one day longer than a year ago. items.title: Kansas City BTR construction has declined from 2023 peak
items.description: HighlightsThe vacancy rate in the Kansas City build-to-rent (BTR) market has declined in each of the past two quarters. Deliveries have slowed, with projects totaling roughly 325 units being completed year to date. In 2025, approximately 800 units came online.Despite a dip during the third quarter, asking rents in the BTR sector rose 3% in the past year to $2,153 per month. Current asking rents for BTR properties are exceeding traditional apartment rents by more than $850 per month while trailing the average monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home by roughly $1,000 per month.After reaching nearly 9% at the start of 2026, vacancy has trended lower in back-to-back quarters. During the past three months, the vacancy rate declined by 30 basis points to 8.1%. Year over year, vacancy is down 10 basis points.Sales activity for build-to-rent properties has been steady in 2026, with one BTR transaction being recorded in each quarter. In transactions where pricing was available, the median price to this point in 2026 is $161,100 per unit. In 2025, the median price was $257,100 per unit.Kansas City build-to-rent market overviewSupply growth in the Kansas City build-to-rent sector continues, but at a slower rate. items.description: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 Texas’ housing market continued to soften in September as rising mortgage rates, inflation, and affordability challenges restrained buyer demand, slowed sales, and kept home-price growth muted. By Yanling Mayer quick links September continued to see a pullback in market momentum, as seasonal cooling combined with rising mortgage rates, rising inflationary pressures, and affordability constraints dampened buyer activity. Existing-home sales declined from a year earlier, and market activity remained subdued. Fewer than two out of every ten homes listed for sale during the month were sold (1.5 homes), highlighting slower inventory turnover and longer marketing times amid challenging demand conditions. Year to date, sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s pace, suggesting housing demand has not deteriorated from last year. Home-price growth remained muted. Statewide home prices were essentially unchanged from a year ago, as gains in a handful of markets were offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Major metropolitan areas, including Austin, Dallas, and San Antonio, continued to experience measurable downward price pressure, while Houston and the Fort Worth metro division showed signs of modest stabilization. On the supply side, inventory levels eased seasonally following their summer peak, consistent with typical market patterns heading into the fall and winter. Nevertheless, overall inventory remains only slightly below peak summer levels, indicating that the inventory condition remains favorable to buyers. Looking ahead, the housing market is expected to remain soft through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates are near current multi-decade highs, limiting purchasing power and sidelining prospective buyers. Unless financing conditions improve meaningfully, housing demand is likely to remain restrained, resulting in slower sales and weak prices. Disclaimer: The September 2026 figures are based on more complete data and have been revised from their initial release. Source: Texas REALTORS® and National Association of REALTORS® and U.S. Census Bureau data In September, Texas recorded 20,200 existing-home sales statewide, down 1.6 percent year over year (YoY). September marked a second consecutive month of YoY sales declines. As of 3Q2026, year-to-date (YTD) sales volume rose 3.3 percent from last year. As of September, median existing-home price was $325,000, softening slightly from August’s $330,000 and unchanged from a year ago. Nationally, seasonally unadjusted existing home sales were down 3.9 percent YoY, a second consecutive month of sales declines, while YTD sales volumes remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace. National median price reached $422,700, maintaining a steady growth pace at about 1.4 percent YoY. September’s new-home sales in U.S. declined 3.4 percent YoY. Inventory turnover was slow at 15 percent, down from 16.2 percent a year ago. At this pace, fewer than two in ten existing homes (1.5 homes) on the market went under contract during the month. The median seller price cut remained similar to a year ago at $15,000, equivalent to roughly 4.5 percent of the initial listing price. items.title: BTR Operators Push For Treasury To Loosen Rules As Consolidation Looms – BisNow
items.description: The build-to-rent sector is facing a second round of wrangling with the government after a hard-fought battle with lawmakers over the summer to keep the industry from facing steep regulations as part of the housing bill that made its way through Congress . BTR operators and industry advocates are pushing for changes to proposed rules from the Department of the Treasury that will dictate how the restrictions on BTR operators from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act are implemented. Operators in the sector say the rules could hamper new development and, regardless of what’s adjusted, expect consolidation to sweep across the sector. “Hopefully that gets adjusted, because that will have a severe impact on capital flows and ultimately the building of new homes and new rental communities,” Richard Ross , CEO of Atlanta-based Quinn Residences , said of the proposed rules. Unsplash/Michael Tuszynski The proposed regulations require large institutional investors, which are defined in the original legislation as firms with at least 350 single-family rental units, to adopt written BTR programs before they purchase a community and would preclude BTR operators from purchasing properties more than 18 months after the home received its certificate of occupancy. Ross, whose firm has developed or purchased 5,200 homes across 34 communities since its founding in 2020, wrote in a letter submitted as a public comment to Treasury that it can frequently take two years or more to stabilize a newly built community. The two new rules would make it more difficult for homebuilders to sell excess inventory to build-to-rent operators, hampering activity in a pool of properties that BTR operators have long dipped into, Ross told Bisnow . His letter was one of more than 100 public comments filed so far. Other operators and industry groups, including the nonpartisan trade association National Rental Home Council , are still crafting their own submissions, CEO Adrianne Todman said. The public comment period closes on Nov. 23. “The Treasury Department has put forward some thoughtful rules where they're trying to thread the needle very carefully by making sure they are properly implementing the legislative ban on investors being able to buy homes but also making sure that it's not having any detrimental impacts to the housing marketplace and particularly the rental marketplace,” Todman said. The push to shift the rules follows the first bout of uncertainty that shrouded the BTR sector when the Road to Housing legislation was originally being debated. The bill debuted with strict restrictions on the BTR business model that threatened to upend the sector. It took intense lobbying for the rules to shift. Investment in the sector was severely scaled back during that debate, as investors waited to see what the final legislation would include. “When there was a threat to being able to build new rental supply via build-to-rent, we saw that there was millions of dollars and thousands of units that went on the sidelines and that those resources were frozen,” Todman said. “Those resources are thawing out a bit, and we want to make sure that they thaw out even more.” The push for clear guidelines gained new momentum after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Some senators-elect ran on campaigns explicitly against corporate ownership of homes, including James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa. Talarico’s website includes a call to “ban Wall Street from buying up housing stock to enrich wealthy investors while making it harder for families to afford homes,” and Turek’s platform includes a call to ban private equity firms from purchasing single-family homes. The Road to Housing legislation adds new compliance standards and an element of federal oversight, including public reporting requirements for large operators, that are expected to lead to a wave of buyouts and mergers across the sector. The consolidation is likely coming regardless of where Treasury lands on its rules, as smaller players are squeezed by costs that large operators that benefit from economies of scale can more easily absorb. “You put it all together, it's just a tougher backdrop for them to really justify their existence,” said Haendel St. Juste , equity research analyst at Mizuho , who upgraded the two major publicly traded single-family rental firms to outperform in September. Unsplash/Nate Johnston New compliance costs for operators with at least 350 units but not thousands will raise operating costs for smaller BTR firms around the same time that the private equity funds backing those platforms reach the end of their lives. A substantial amount of the debt backing private BTR and SFR firms was issued around five to seven years ago and is reaching the end of its natural life cycle, leaving operators facing significantly higher debt service costs to stay in business, St. Juste said. Nontraded SFR REIT VineBrook Homes Trust suspended share buybacks earlier this month after ending a tender offer that drew three times as many shares as the REIT sought to buy. VineBrook, which has 20,500 units in 21 states, flagged an upcoming $650.8M debt maturity within a year as a driving factor behind the shift in strategy. For Invitation Homes and American Homes 4 Rent , the two biggest publicly traded single-family rental firms, the legislation creates a unique and sizable rollup opportunity, St. Juste wrote in a September analysis. The two REITs have trailed the broader REIT index by about 13 percentage points this year, according to Mizuho’s September report, and investors see upside potential in the wide gap that exists between the firms’ public valuations and the value of the properties in their portfolios. The REITs have been using that gap to sell homes and buy back stock at an attractive valuation, a trend that is expected to continue into 2027. items.title: Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows
items.description: The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction. The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021 : when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%. Building permits From Census : Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October. As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle. Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive. Builders confidence at multiyear lows One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years. Conclusion Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more. Related More:

items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for October 2026. November 20, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: The new home market has slipped into underperformance October marked another step backward for the new home market. Sales declined 3.1% month-over-month and 11.7% year-over-year, a considerably steeper annual decline than September's 4.6% drop. The weakness was widespread, with pending sales declining year-over-year across all of Zonda's select markets. The national Zonda Market Ranking also slipped into slightly underperforming territory for the first time since December 2022. The latest figures reinforce what builders have been telling us for months. Zonda's October builder sentiment survey found that 86% of builders reported slower-than-expected demand, up from 84% in September. In their comments, builders pointed to declining traffic, limited buyer urgency, and growing frustration with the effectiveness of incentives. “One of the biggest challenges for builders right now is generating enough buyer interest in the first place,” said Sarah Bonnarens, director of economic research for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Builders still have an advantage when it comes to pricing and financing flexibility, but those tools can only do so much when buyer traffic is down. The challenge is keeping sales moving without putting even more pressure on margins.” The annual decline in new home sales deepened Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 638,568 new homes sold in October on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a decline of 3.1% from last month and a drop of 11.7% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 50,770 homes were sold, 11.6% lower than last year and 2.8% below the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In October, 64% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 83% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so they will underrepresent overall usage. All select markets saw PSI fall YOY Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The October PSI came in at 122.8, representing an 11.4% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 29.5% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales decreased 1.9%. The markets that held up the best relative to last year were Minneapolis (-0.3%), Charlotte (-1.1%), and Tampa (-3.5%). Minneapolis was down compared to the last year but grew 10.2% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Los Angeles/OC (-31.4%), Riverside/San Bernardino (-28.4%), and Denver (-26.3%). On a monthly basis, Minneapolis, Sacramento, and Denver were the best performing markets. The National ZMR dropped to slightly underperforming In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Get ZMR Maps The National ZMR index came in at 87.4 in October, which indicated a slightly underperforming market. This marked the first downgrade to the national overall rating since January 2025. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 10% average, and 90% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 5% were overperforming , 25% were average , and 70% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. Price cuts persist in the two lower tiers National home prices increased 2.7% year-over-year for high-end homes to $951,036. Meanwhile, modest declines in the entry-level and move-up segments come as builders continue to adjust pricing and product offerings in response to affordability challenges and softer demand. Nonfarm employment held at just over 2.0 million workers, while the local unemployment rate climbed 30 basis points (bps) year-over-year (YOY) to 4.1%. At just 10 bps below the U.S. average of 4.2%, the gap between local and national labor market conditions narrowed, reflecting a departure from the metro’s longstanding pattern of outperforming national employment trends. items.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
items.description: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012 by ATTOM Team | Nov 19, 2026 | Mortgage Origination , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Home purchase lending falls 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans; Refinance lending drops 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans IRVINE, Calif. – Nov. 19, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report for the third quarter of 2026, showing purchase and refinance lending slowed from the previous quarter as mortgage rates climbed and home purchase loans fell to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012. A total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (1 to 4 units) were originated in the third quarter, down 12 percent from the previous quarter and 15 percent from a year earlier. Total loan volume reached $498.1 billion, down 15 percent quarterly and 12 percent year-over-year. The quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending. Purchase loans fell 9 percent from the previous quarter to 729,968, marking the lowest third-quarter total since 2012. Purchase loans were down 12 percent from a year earlier, even as the average purchase loan amount rose 3 percent over the same period to $411,756. “The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.” Purchase lending slips quarterly in most markets Purchase lending totaled $300.6 billion in the third quarter, down 10 percent from the previous quarter and 10 percent below year-ago levels. Purchase loans accounted for 56.5 percent of all purchase and refinance originations, up from 54.5 percent in both the second quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. Purchase activity declined quarterly in 73.6 percent of analyzed metro areas with a population of 200,000 or more and sufficient data. Among metros with populations above 1 million, the largest quarterly increases were in Buffalo, NY (up 61 percent); Memphis, TN (up 50 percent); Rochester, NY (up 32 percent); New York, NY (up 22 percent); and Hartford, CT (up 20 percent). The steepest quarterly drops among large metros were in Salt Lake City, UT; New Orleans, LA; Denver, CO; Atlanta, GA; and Richmond, VA. Refinancing activity falls sharply quarter-over-quarter Refinancing activity fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans, the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2024, and was 19 percent below the third quarter of 2025. Refinance originations accounted for 43.5 percent of all purchase and refinance loans, down from 45.5 percent in both the previous quarter and a year earlier. Refinance lending declined quarterly in 89.4 percent of analyzed metro areas, with the steepest quarterly drops among large metros in San Jose, CA; Dallas, TX; San Francisco, CA; Austin, TX; and Louisville, KY. FHA and VA loan shares decline quarterly Loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration accounted for 15.7 percent of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from 16.1 percent in the second quarter and 17.9 percent a year earlier. items.description: Multifamily Rebalancing Advances Nov 17, 2026 | 4 min read U.S. Multifamily Capital Markets | Q3 2026 Multifamily fundamentals continued to rebalance as occupancy edged higher, rent recovery broadened, and the construction pipeline contracted, creating a firmer foundation heading into 2027. Download the full report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. David Goodhue Executive Managing Director | Boston & Head of Multifamily Capital Markets | U.S Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research View All [5] Experts Share Article Top Highlights Occupancy continued to improve, edging higher to 95.7% despite more subdued leasing activity in the third quarter. Demand moderated from the exceptional second-quarter pace, with absorption trailing new deliveries but remaining well above year-ago levels. The development pipeline continued to contract, improving the longer-term supply outlook while near-term pressure remains concentrated in select markets. Rent recovery broadened across markets, with 40 of the Top 60 markets posting positive annual rent growth. Capital markets remain selective, as underlying transaction activity and pricing continue to reflect price discovery rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Key Statistics Multifamily fundamentals remain resilient as the market continues to work through recent supply additions and the development pipeline moderates. Occupancy Remains Resilient National occupancy remained healthy in Q3 2026 as markets continued to absorb recently delivered units. While conditions vary across geographies, supply-constrained markets continue to demonstrate particularly strong operating fundamentals, while higher-supply markets remain more competitive. Source: Colliers Research, RealPage, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Rent Recovery Broadens Rent performance improved across a broader share of markets during the third quarter, signaling a more widespread recovery in pricing conditions. Performance remains uneven, however, with supply levels and local demand continuing to drive meaningful differences between markets. Supply Risk Remains Concentrated The national development pipeline continued to contract during the third quarter as financing challenges, elevated construction costs, and capital constraints limited new development. While the pullback should ease supply pressure nationally over time, several markets still face elevated construction pipelines that will continue to influence near-term performance. Capital Markets Navigate a Selective Recovery Investment activity continues to reflect a market in transition. Multifamily transaction volume reached $114.1 billion in Q3 2026, but the increase primarily reflected an entity-level merger rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Excluding entity-level transactions, volume declined 7% to $44.5 billion, while apartment pricing remained under pressure. Investors continue to prioritize durable cash flow, realistic acquisition pricing, and manageable refinancing exposure as the market works through continued price discovery. Source: Colliers Research, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Sector Spotlight: Seniors Housing Seniors housing is benefiting from a combination of powerful demographic demand, improving operating performance, and constrained new supply. Growth in the older U.S. population is expanding the long-term demand base for independent living, assisted living, and nursing care, while limited development is supporting occupancy and rent fundamentals. Capital markets activity is also strengthening as investors respond to improving fundamentals and the sector's long-term demographic outlook. The report examines operating trends, regional performance, transaction activity, and the investment landscape across seniors housing and care. Looking Ahead Multifamily enters the final months of 2026 with healthy occupancy, a shrinking development pipeline, and a broader rent recovery, creating a more constructive operating backdrop. At the same time, capital markets remain selective, and refinancing pressure continues to create challenges and opportunities across the sector. Heading into 2027, the pace of new supply, local demand trends, and financing conditions will remain critical to determining where operating performance and investment opportunities strengthen most. U.S. Market Overviews The report features key statistics across the Top 60 U.S. multifamily markets, along with detailed spotlights on 15 select markets: Baltimore, Cincinnati, Denver, Greensboro, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, Memphis, Nassau County, Northern/Central New Jersey, Orange County, Pittsburgh, Richmond, San Diego, St. Louis, and Washington, D.C. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.28% as of November 19, 2026, up from last week when it averaged 7.11%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.26%. Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: A conflict of interest
items.description: Non-QM loans are part of the equation helping investors expand their footprint in the property market. Financing edge: Five-year, interest-only loans can maximize rental margins over short hold periods. Market shift: As institutional investment retreats, mom-and-pop buyers stepped in, acquiring 20% more homes than they sold. Buyer fallout: Heavy investor demand keeps prices and rents high, contributing to locking gig and freelance workers out of ownership. Millions of Americans now embrace freelancing, small-business ownership, or gig-economy careers, but the industry hasn’t widely adopted lending structures that correspond to this shift. Add to that dynamic the increasingly unaffordable price tag for homes, and many would-be homeowners are stuck as renters. Many are renting from similarly minded entrepreneurs: mom-and-pop investors. The difference is that investors are turning to non-QM mortgages to finance property transactions, according to Cotatlity data. Many are doing so to take advantage of interest-only payments. The five-year flip The U.S. housing market offers an ideal proposition to small investors. Rents have increased 25% in the last five years, the federal government has curbed institutional investment, and home equity continues to rise. Investors are responding by reasserting their presence in markets across the U.S. Cotality data shows that the share of investors making home purchases has climbed since mid-2022 and now represents about a third of all transactions. Small investors represent about half of that transaction volume. Investment transactions occur frequently, making them an ideal candidate for interest-only loans. Nearly half of investor hold onto a property for five years or less — that precise timeframe makes an interest-only mortgage worth the equity tradeoff. Most interest-only loans have an initial period of five years before principal repayment begins where monthly commitments are reduced to create wider profit margins on rents. While investors who finance this way won’t reap the benefits of accrued equity, they can profit from the persistently high home prices and a tight inventory that makes short-term commitments profitable. How long does each investor type hold property Data source: Cotality, 2026 The U.S. is short 4.7 million homes . The ones that are available are in high demand. Add in mortgage rates near 7%, and affordability is being tested at its limits. Home prices reflect that squeeze. That dynamic has allowed investors in states like California, where they buy over a third of all homes, to profit on investments financed by interest-only loans. Investors nearly doubled the number of purchases they made in Los Angeles between Q1 and Q2 2026. Home prices jumped 2% during that period. This localized surge in investment is colliding directly with broader national price pressures—a dynamic we analyzed in our piece, Bend It Like Buyers. In major metros, that friction has created a stalemate between buyers and sellers, leaving the door open to more financially flexible investors. Many blame Wall Street. Institutional investors ban themselves Injecting corporate-backed demand into a market where local buyers are already stretched, extends even the most flexible buyers past their breaking point. Local residents who are priced out of home purchases find themselves competing with incoming industrial contractors for the exact same rental inventory. The resulting rent escalation drives up investor yields in the short term, but it simultaneously compresses local household purchasing power and accelerates affordability risk. That has a direct influence on local markets. In states like California, Texas, and Georgia, where investors buy over a third of all homes, prices have risen disproportionately. In Texas, home prices jumped 38% as investor share climbed to 31% between 2020 and 2023. In Georgia, prices jumped 54% alongside an investor share increase to 29%. But the passage of the 21 st Century ROAD to Housing Bill disrupted that playbook. Even before the passage of the bill, Cotality data shows that institutional investment contracted from around 250 home purchases a week to 100. Mom-and-pop investors filled the gap. Small-time landlords entered a market where equity was on the rise, which allowed them to build a cash cushion to insulate them from current high-interest rates and create wider profit margins that allow them to redeploy capital elsewhere. When that equity cushion is layered atop monthly rental income profit, these landlords can offset systemic hurdles such as interest rates and rising home insurance costs. Much of that extra capital is going into increasing their market share. Small mom-and-pop investors purchased 20% more homes than they offloaded last year, according to Cotality data. Their persistent presence is reshaping the housing market. Main street moves in Across the country, investors are the ones with the financial wherewithal to purchase homes in the current high-cost, high-rate environment. This is contributing to keeping costs — from home prices to rents — elevated and widening the gap for aspiring homeowners. Some renters will be blocked from homeowership by these costs. Others will bend and stretch to make the homeownership math work. Some will look to non-QM mortgages themselves. Forward-looking lenders who are optimizing for long-term growth will cater to both sides. There is now a path forward. It may be unconventional, but it is a door through which an increasing number of investors and homeowners are stepping to make the dream of homeownership a reality. items.description: Single-Family Starts Post Modest Monthly Rebound Amid Challenging Conditions November 18, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Single-family housing starts edged up in October but still posted the year’s second-slowest pace, as builders face elevated financing and material costs, persistent labor shortages, and buyers holding back amid economic uncertainty. Single-family permits, the most important indicator in this report, declined to their lowest monthly pace since January 2023, reflecting continued weakness in single-family construction. Overall housing starts increased 9.9% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.31 million units, according to a report from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the U.S. Census Bureau. This pace reflects the number of housing units builders would begin over the next twelve months if October’s activity were sustained. Within the total, single-family starts increased 4.0% to an 864,000 seasonally adjusted annual rate. However, single-family starts were down 3.2% compared to October 2025. On a year-to-date basis, single-family starts were down 4.6%, reflecting continued challenges facing home builders . Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units. Multifamily starts, which include apartment buildings and condominiums, increased 23.6% from September to October to an annualized 445,000 pace. The three-month moving average for multifamily construction has trended lower to 401,000 units, but activity is 17.1% higher compared to year-earlier levels. Regionally, on a year-to-date basis, combined single-family and multifamily starts were 3.8% higher in the Northeast, 0.2% higher in the South, 0.7% lower in the Midwest, and 6.7% lower in the West. Single-family starts declined across all four regions, reflecting ongoing challenges amid elevated construction costs and persistent housing affordability pressures. The total number of housing units under construction stood at 1.27 million in October, down 3.0% from a year earlier. Single-family homes under construction stood at 581,000 units, a 2.5% year-over-year decline. Multifamily units under construction slowed to 691,000 units, down from peaks above 1 million units in December 2023 and 3.5% lower than a year ago. Single-family completions edged up to an annualized rate of about 900,000 units but came down 10.7% from a year earlier. Multifamily completions for buildings with five or more units declined 9.0% year-over-year to a 362,000-unit pace. However, compared to the previous month, completions were up 9.0%. On a year-to-date basis, total completions across both sectors were down 12.3%. Looking ahead, overall permits declined 7.4% in October to an annualized rate of 1.3 million units. Single-family permits declined 8.7% to a 772,000-unit rate, the lowest level since January 2023. Single-family permits were down 12.9% compared to October 2025 and are down 4.2% on a year-to-date basis. Multifamily permits declined 5.3% to an annualized 523,000 pace and are down 1.7% from a year earlier. Looking at regional permit data on a year-to-date basis, total permits were 8.7% higher in the Northeast, 2.0% higher in the Midwest, but 2.5% lower in the West and 4.4% lower in the South. items.title: This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks
items.description: This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks Published on November 17th, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates climbed last week following surprising commentary from the Fed potentially hinting at more hikes to come, but there are plenty of opportunities for Fed speakers to clarify their views this week. Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target. Notably, a few hours before CPI, Fed Governor Christopher Waller came out with some surprising remarks, putting a 50 bps December hike on the table as a possibility if inflation came in high, which it did. Before he spoke, markets would have assumed an inflation report like the one we got would lead to a guaranteed 25 bps hike. Now markets are assuming the 25 bps hike happens and pricing in some possibility for a larger hike. Subsequent remarks from other Fed officials backed off the 50 bps hike but showed possible support for another hike in January. Previously, markets had assumed that the next hike would happen in March. The net effect of all of this is that markets are now pricing in almost two additional rate hikes by mid-2027 than they were previously, which is why mortgage rates increased last week. The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy. Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand. Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much. Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow. items.title: The Blue Wave Has Foreign Capital Dipping Its Toes Back Into U.S. Commercial Real Estate
items.description: Trade wars , inflation and prolonged conflict in the Middle East made foreign investors increasingly cautious about the U.S., even as cross-border transactions rebounded globally. But in the aftermath of Democratic Party victories in midterm elections across the country, overseas capital may once again be warming to American real estate, fund managers said at Bisnow ’s New York City State of the Market event on Thursday. Unsplash/Amelia “The sentiment toward the U.S. was very, very negative, and even since two weeks ago, we've seen some thawing in those pools of capital that were pulling back from the U.S. for the past couple of years,” Vistria Group partner Sherry Wang said onstage. That marks a sharp reversal from earlier this year, when Wang said some foreign funds rescinded mandates to invest in the U.S., citing geopolitical concerns even as they continued to “believe in the underlying real estate for the most part.” In the first half of the year, cross-border investment in commercial real estate surged 56% to $71.8B globally, Reuters reported . Most of that increase came from Asia and Europe. Singapore ranked first among individual markets, attracting $8.7B in investment. The U.S. captured a smaller-than-usual slice of the global market. In the 12 months leading up to September, the country attracted $28B, a 15% share of all cross-border investment, according to a report by Colliers . That lagged below its five-year average of nearly 19%. Between 2022 and 2024, many investors held allocations in the U.S. steady, before decreasing their targets by 10 basis points in 2025, according to the Association of Foreign Investors in Real Estate . In an AFIRE survey conducted throughout July and August, 53% of respondents, representing more than $4T in global assets, said they plan to decrease or not change their overall U.S. allocations. That’s even though 58% of those same respondents had a positive view of the U.S. economy. Those with a negative outlook more than doubled from the same time last year, from 12.5% to nearly 27%, with more than 90% of respondents citing the U.S. political landscape as the reason why. Bisnow/Sasha Jones Cole Schotz’s Robert DiPisa, Besen Partners’ Sam Finkler, Legal 1031 Exchange’s Todd Pajonas, Muss Development’s Jason Muss and Vistria Group’s Sherry Wang Few of the factors that stood in the way of dealmaking — like interest rates and construction costs — have changed since Election Day, but there is a greater sense of certainty and, in some parts of the U.S. economy, positivity. In its first survey since the midterms , Oxford Economics found that U.S. consumer sentiment rose and year-ahead inflation expectations fell by a full percentage point to 3.7%, the most substantial decline since the start of the Iran war . Having a blue Congress and a red White House is likely to create new hurdles that block laws, budgets or appointments from approval. For the real estate industry, that may not be such a bad thing, Legal 1031 Exchange President Todd Pajonas said during the event, held at Convene One Liberty Plaza. “There's not going to be any change to the tax code, which drives a lot of business. There's not going to be huge swings in monetary policy. We're not going to see the huge tariffs . We're going to see an end, hopefully, to the conflict in the Middle East because there's not going to be the political will to do it,” Pajonas said. “I think the next two years are going to look somewhat better because of political gridlock.” AFIRE CEO Gunnar Branson told GlobeSt earlier this month that his members expressed a similar sentiment to him on the day of the election. Real estate played a prominent role in November’s election, with housing affordability and data center backlash taking center stage. Across the country, a series of Republican stronghold states flipped, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska, in some cases giving Democrats control for the first time in decades . In New York City, where several candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America won, landlords especially fear tightening tenant protections. “You look at COPA , that was just enacted. Every now and then — I don't even want to say it out loud — the commercial rent control bill rears its ugly head,” Besen Partners Managing Director Sam Finkler said. “It's really local policy agenda and interest rates that are going to play out over the next couple of years.” Bisnow/Sasha Jones Adler & Stachenfeld’s Kim Le, BGO’s Abbe Franchot Borok, Silverstein Properties’ Jeffrey Deitrich, Pimco's Michael Givner and NAI Global’s Arthur Milston Even with increased regulatory scrutiny, New York City continues to be one of the most supply-constrained markets in the country. Foreign investors may take a moment to recalibrate, but they are unlikely to be dissuaded in the long run, panelists said. “I don't think there's any foreign capital that has redlined, crossed off New York because of the political climate,” NAI Global Senior Managing Director and Head of Capital Markets Arthur Milston said. “In fact, I think most people view that typically as transient.” Manhattan’s median rent reached $5,279 per month in October, up 6% year-over-year, while vacancy fell to 1.3%, the lowest level since March 2020, according to Corcoran . The city has led the country in office recovery and is one of the few markets where new office supply is being delivered. Globally, the under-construction office pipeline was 580M SF in the third quarter, 45% below its 2017 peak and its lowest level in a decade, according to Cushman & Wakefield .
