items.title: Some FHA borrowers pay mortgage insurance for a decade or more. There's an industry push to change the rules
items.description: Read more CNBC personal finance coverage How to get Anthropic stock — without buying the IPO There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The push, which revives a longstanding mortgage industry request, also comes several weeks after President Donald Trump issued an executive order that included calling for the launch of a federal pilot program that would cancel mortgage insurance on certain conventional loans once borrowers meet equity requirements. The order would apply generally to future loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — two government-sponsored enterprises that purchase qualifying mortgages from lenders and resell them as bundled securities. It wouldn't apply to FHA loans. Here's who uses FHA mortgages FHA mortgages are issued by private lenders but insured by the federal government, which protects lenders against losses if a borrower defaults. The loans are designed to make homeownership more accessible, particularly for borrowers with limited savings for a down payment or with lower credit scores. Affordability challenges persist in the housing market, with elevated home prices and mortgage rates putting homeownership out of reach for many prospective buyers. Existing homeowners are also facing rising costs alongside their mortgages, including property taxes and homeowners insurance amid overall high inflation . About 83% of new FHA purchase loans went to first-time homebuyers in the most recent fiscal year, according to the FHA report to Congress. Altogether, the FHA insured more than 8.4 million mortgages as of Sept. 30. The median age of first-time buyers is 40, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors. watch now VIDEO 0:31 00:31 Can you afford to buy a home? Personal Finance FHA loans also require borrowers to pay mortgage insurance regardless of the size of their down payment. Under current rules established in 2013 , FHA borrowers with a down payment that's less than 10% of the loan must pay mortgage insurance premiums for the duration of the loan. Those who put 10% or more down pay that insurance for 11 years. Borrowers generally pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium and an annual premium, which is typically divided into monthly payments. The upfront premium is usually 1.75% of the base loan amount and can be financed into the mortgage. For many borrowers with 30-year FHA loans, the annual premium is 0.55% of the outstanding loan balance. Conventional mortgages generally don't require mortgage insurance unless the loan is for more than 80% of the home's value. In 2022, the premium typically ranged from 0.58% to 1.86% annually, according to Fannie Mae . If those borrowers have to pay mortgage insurance, they can typically request its removal once they've built 20% equity in the home, or it is automatically canceled when their loan drops to 78% of the original value. Proposals from the mortgage industry The mortgage industry has floated two different proposals. One would reduce the rate that applies to FHA mortgage insurance. For example, the Mortgage Bankers Association recently suggested a rate reduction of 20 basis points , which would lower the standard 0.55% rate to 0.35% for new borrowers. For example: On a $350,000 mortgage, a 0.55% rate generally translates into $1,925 annually, or about $160 monthly, at the start of the loan. As the principal owed slowly goes down over time through a borrower's monthly payments, so does that mortgage insurance amount. At 0.35%, the annual premium would be $1,225 at the start of the loan, or $102 monthly — a difference of $58 per month. The FHA last cut that rate in 2023 , when it was reduced from 0.85%. At the time, HUD estimated that affected borrowers would save an average of $800 annually. However, in the FHA's new report to Congress, the agency noted that the 2023 cut has reduced the fund's revenue, contributing to a decline in its capital ratio. The other industry proposal would implement auto-cancellation of premiums once the loan balance fell to 78% of the home's original value at purchase — in other words, the same as for Fannie- and Freddie-backed mortgages. Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown. Michael Farrell National Association of Mortgage Brokers "Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown," said Michael Farrell, president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, a trade group that generally has supported the cancellation proposal. "NAMB believes that cancellation at 78% protects the [FHA insurance fund], because premiums can restart if the [capital] ratio ever falls to 2%," Farrell said. FHA mortgages received that treatment from 2001 through 2013, but the agency eliminated it to shore up its insurance fund after financial reserves deteriorated over time following the housing market crash, which led to the 2008 financial crisis. Whether the proposals will go anywhere this time is uncertain. HUD, which oversees the FHA, did not respond to a CNBC email seeking more information. items.title: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks
items.description: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks Former CISA Director Chris Krebs told OPTECH attendees that they need to know which AI tools employees and vendors are using. Published Nov. 20, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Chris Krebs speaks at OPTECH 2026 on Nov. 17. Les Shaver/Multifamily Dive Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . The Real Estate Technology & Transformation Center picked a helluva time to hold OPTECH 2026, which ran from Nov. 16 to 18 at the MGM Grand Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas. In the week before the conference began, a Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook , angering users worldwide (including this one). The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, while Workday also had a much less high-profile outage that day. For people like me who don’t like getting on planes (it’s not about crashing; it's about not having control, as I often tell my wife), the ground stop was alarming. The week of OPTECH, outages followed at JPMorgan Chase, Apple, the National Security Agency and, to my chagrin, briefly, United. That one led to a minor freakout as I walked the OPTECH expo floor. My apologies to those of you who chose to speak with me. In an extremely fortunate bit of planning, RETTC actually booked former United States Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Chris Krebs to speak on Tuesday. It wasn’t surprising to learn that he tore up his original presentation to focus on current events. With the FAA having a hardware-related shutdown, Krebs’ explanation for the majority of the disruptions was that artificial intelligence is helping firms find software flaws. As they scramble to patch issues, outages occur. “We're going to have more outages,” Krebs said. “But I also think we're going to learn from every one of these. So there are always lessons learned, whether it's from the Chase, United [and] from Microsoft.” However, he emphasized this won’t be a short-term process. “The good news is we're almost done, right?” Krebs said. “Nope. We're in like the second inning of this ball game.” How apartment firms can fortify their systems For apartment firms looking to protect their own systems, Krebs said the first place to start is by peeking under the hood and seeing what’s happening in their own companies. Find out what AI tools employees are using. “You have a pretty significant risk at that point of a PII [personally identifiable information] or other sensitive data leak,” Krebs said. “So you've got to be very cognizant of any sort of AI use in your environment, what it touches, including the secrets, the keys that it has access to. That can get out, and then you've got a completely different problem with a data breach.” Apartment firms also need to know who inside the organization owns the problem if something goes wrong and where the kill switch is. If “it's either misbehaving or the vendor is a jerk, and I want to turn it off, how do I do that?” Krebs said. Suppliers also deserve scrutiny, according to Krebs. “You're going to have to extend that review and analysis to your vendors because every one of your vendors is probably using AI, and I'm not quite sure if they're telling you,” he said. “So, vendors in the room, be transparent.” Above all, companies that develop their own products need to know their exposure and quickly patch any issues, which is reportedly happening across the broader economy right now. “If you do develop code, and a lot of you do for some of your proprietary products, make sure that you're using AI to scan the code that's being developed,” Krebs said. “Now, don't just grab some random open source model. There are specific harnesses and products that are developed specifically for secure coding.” Krebs’ points struck a chord with me. In the midst of the chaos, it may be a good time for apartment executives to look at their own systems and determine what happens if there’s an outage. While I can’t control United’s schedule from the OPTECH exhibition floor (in case you’re wondering, I made my flight and am writing this final paragraph from the friendly skies above Champaign, Illinois), multifamily leaders can prepare for what’s coming. items.description: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. ' data-gallery='global-photo' data-toggle="lightbox"> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. items.title: October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle
items.description: October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle by John Yellig November 18, 2026 October's pending home sales fell to what could be the nadir of this housing cycle — or it could represent just another step on the path of many would-be homeowners giving up altogether, the National Association of REALTORS® said. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” Pending sales fell 4.7% from September and 16.7% from October 2026 on a national basis. Regionally, contract signings were down across the board on monthly and yearly bases. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun said. Even the strongest markets in recent memory saw declines. These metros saw the smallest declines: Cincinnati, Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, Texas (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Connecticut (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, Indiana (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, Illinois-Indiana (-11.9%) Pittsburgh (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, Tennessee (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, New York (-12.7%) Jacksonville, Florida (-12.8%) Cleveland (-12.8%) “Buyers everywhere are running into the same affordability wall, with contract signings falling in every region," First American Financial Senior Economist Sam Williamson said. "The South and West each dropped more than 6%, the Midwest slipped nearly 3%, and the Northeast barely moved. From a year ago, every region is down by double digits, with the West off roughly 20%." items.title: Pretium Expands Real Estate Debt Platform
items.description: Pretium Expands Real Estate Debt Platform November 19, 2026 --> Addition of Hilltop Capital Partners Enables the Firm to Deploy Capital to the U.K. Housing Market NEW YORK, November 19, 2026 – Pretium, a specialized investment firm with approximately $70 billion in assets under management, today announced it is expanding its residential real estate debt platform, further enabling the flow of capital to real estate investors, developers, and homebuilders. Since launching its residential debt platform in December 2024, Pretium has lent approximately $8 billion for the purpose of new housing construction and the renovation of existing homes. Building on its existing model, Pretium is adding the team from Hilltop Capital Partners (“Hilltop”), a specialized U.K.-based institutional capital advisor, investment manager and principal lender, to its vertically integrated residential real estate platform. Led by Paul Oberschneider and Tiger Craft, Hilltop has grown into a leading platform for residential development finance across the U.K since its founding in 2019. “The U.K. faces a housing shortage of approximately four to five million homes, and the Hilltop team has built an impressive platform supporting homebuilders, developers and sponsors with flexible, solutions-oriented capital,” said Jonathan Pruzan, Co-President at Pretium. “This expansion is a natural extension of the model we’ve built in the U.S., and we are pleased to welcome the Hilltop team to Pretium. Our real estate debt platform provides much-needed capital to grow the housing stock, while delivering value to our investors.” “U.K. homebuilders need capital that understands development risk and the full ecosystem of finance. Joining the Pretium ecosystem provides us the scale the U.K. homebuilder market requires right now, and I’m excited about what this means for the business in the years ahead,” said Paul Oberschneider, Chairman of Hilltop. "We are thrilled to be joining Pretium. The firm's depth of talent and focus on residential markets make this a natural fit for Hilltop. This gives us the infrastructure and backing to deliver flexible financing to U.K. residential developers and sponsors with greater speed, scale and certainty of execution," said Tiger Craft, CEO of Hilltop. About Pretium Pretium is a specialized investment firm focused on U.S. residential real estate equity and credit. Pretium was founded in 2012 and has built an integrated analytical and operational ecosystem within the U.S. housing and credit markets and believes that its insight and experience within these markets create a strategic advantage. Pretium’s platform has approximately $70 billion in assets and employs 7,000 people across 45+ offices as of June 30, 2026, including its New York headquarters, Miami, London, Abu Dhabi, Bangalore, Seoul and Sydney. Please visit www.pretium.com for additional information. About Hilltop Founded in 2019, Hilltop Credit Partners Limited, trading as Hilltop Capital Partners, is a London-based real estate credit investment adviser and principal lender, focused on providing capital solutions to residential property developers across the UK and Europe. Funds advised by Hilltop have provided c. $300 million in debt funding to support the construction of over 1,000 residential units across the UK. ### Media Contact Brenna Karp Pretium [email protected]

items.title: MLSs file response to Compass effort in lawsuit
items.description: MLSs file response to Compass effort in lawsuit by Emily Marek November 19, 2026 The seven MLSs that filed a joint lawsuit against Compass last month submitted an update in response to the brokerage's dismissal efforts. Following Compass’ dismissal effort, the seven MLSs that filed a joint lawsuit against the mega-brokerage last month have submitted an update to United States District Judge Mary Kay Vyskocil. The MLSs are attempting to block Compass’ Nov. 13 petition to dismiss the case or spread the suit across multiple jurisdictions, arguing the latter action would be inefficient and costly. “Compass’ effort to scatter this dispute across multiple courts would create unnecessary complexity and expense without changing the fundamental issue at stake,” wrote Jeff Bosch, who took over as CEO of the Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service on Oct. 26. “We are defending cooperation rules that promote fair competition, give buyers broader access to available homes and help sellers reach more potential buyers. We believe these rules are lawful and procompetitive, and we look forward to defending them in court.” The seven MLSs involved in the suit — ARMLS, bridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS, MLSListings and REcolorado — maintain that the proceedings should stay in New York, the location of Compass’ headquarters. In addition to Compass’ Nov. 13 filing on ARMLS et al. v. Compass, the brokerage filed separate lawsuits against all seven MLSs — and eight others — on Nov. 12. items.title: Portman kicks off construction of Brookside Village mixed-use community in Alpharetta
items.description: Portman kicks off construction of Brookside Village mixed-use community in Alpharetta by John Yellig November 19, 2026 The project includes 335 apartments and 75 for-sale townhomes, alongside 50,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Via Portman. Portman broke ground on Brookside Village, a new mixed-use community in Alpharetta that will bring 335 apartments and 75 for-sale townhomes to market alongside 50,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. The project represents the redevelopment of a 20-acre office park on Old Milton Parkway and will see the demolition of one of two office buildings. The other one, a 135,000-square-foot building, will be retained. The community will be anchored by Georgia State University’s Alpharetta Campus and its new Panther Quad. Another 375 townhomes from Toll Brothers , Empire Communities and Providence Group will be developed next to the site, for a total of 450 for-sale townhomes in the area. “This is a significant milestone for Brookside Village, marking the beginning of a major reinvention of a well-located but aging office park,” said Mike Greene, managing director of mixed-use development for Portman. “Our partnership with the city of Alpharetta has been instrumental in finding creative solutions to revitalize the campus and transform it into a walkable and amenity-rich district with new homes, restaurants and public space that will serve the community.” Portman is partnering with equity-investment partner EBSCO Real Estate to develop Brookside Village. The project is expected to open in 2029. “Across the country, suburban office parks built for a different era are ready for their next chapter,” Portman Chairman and CEO Ambrish Baisiwala said. “With its strong economy and forward-thinking city leadership, Alpharetta is the right place to show what suburban office redevelopment can look like in this real estate cycle.” Read More Related to This Post Parkland Communities secures $50M development financing, begins Highland Brook in Dacula Bleak house: Builder confidence hits 14-year low in November Ashton Woods names Nicholas Czar SVP of sales Traton Homes begins selling at Flowery Branch townhome community Larkspur Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. items.title: Dallas-Fort Worth multifamily rents post first annual gain in three years
items.description: HighlightsDallas-Fort Worth multifamily operating fundamentals improved during the third quarter, with net absorption continuing to outpace new supply by a wide margin. Since 2020, the market has absorbed more than 172,000 units, underscoring the depth of sustained demand.Asking rents rose 1.0% during the third quarter to $1,512 per month. Rents were up 0.5% year over year, marking the first annual increase since the third quarter of 2023.Vacancy ended the quarter at 6.0%, down 10 basis points from the prior three months and 20 basis points year over year.Among year-to-date transactions with disclosed pricing, the median sale price was $162,100 per unit. Per-unit pricing levels have remained within a tight range for the past several years, while current cap rates are averaging around 5.25%.Dallas-Fort Worth multifamily market overviewDallas-Fort Worth’s operating fundamentals continued to improve during the third quarter. Net absorption totaled roughly 6,600 units, slightly exceeding the 6,400 units delivered during the quarter. Demand was concentrated in Dallas, which accounted for 83% of the Metroplex’s net absorption, up from 79% in the second quarter. Absorption was strongest in the northern suburbs and core neighborhoods, led by Allen/McKinney, Frisco, and Intown Dallas. Year to date, the Metroplex has absorbed more than 26,100 units, outpacing new supply by nearly 40%. The construction pipeline continued to shrink and is now 45% below its early 2023 peak. Vacancy fell for a third consecutive quarter, with declines led by Class C and Class A properties. Average rents rose to $1,512 per month, their third straight quarterly increase. Class A rents again led the way and have now posted annual gains for two straight years.Multifamily investment activity in Dallas-Fort Worth was essentially flat year over year during the third quarter. Year to date, 103 properties with at least 100 units changed hands, down slightly from the same period in 2025. Investment shifted west compared with transactions that closed in 2025. Fort Worth’s share of sales rose to about 20% from 15%, with Arlington and Grand Prairie also gaining ground, while the share of total transactions in the northern suburbs was cut nearly in half to just 12%. Dallas held steady at about 30%. The northern decline reflects fewer sales of newer properties, which drove much of that area's 2025 activity, as loan assumptions and value-add purchases also slowed. The mix also shifted toward distress, as lender-driven sales rose to nine from two a year earlier. The year-to-date median sale price reached roughly $162,100 per unit. Cap rates for newer properties held near 2025 pricing at below 5%, while older garden properties often are approaching 6%.Employment:Local payrolls added 36,200 new positions. Image Employers across the Dallas-Fort Worth area continued to add jobs through the third quarter of 2026, though annual growth slowed. During the past 12 months, local payrolls grew by 0.8%, adding 36,200 new positions.Growth in the professional and business services sector continued to strengthen. Year over year through the third quarter, the sector added 29,100 jobs, representing a 3.7% increase.In September, Morgan Stanley announced plans to establish a new U.S. hub in Dallas. The project represents a $684 million capital investment and is expected to create more than 3,800 jobs.Forecast: Following a period of more modest growth in 2025, the local labor market is forecast to sustain its recent momentum through the remainder of 2026. Approximately 55,000 jobs are projected to be added in 2026, representing a 1.3% increase.Development and permitting:The construction pipeline declined 7% year over year. Image The pace of multifamily deliveries has slowed. Year to date, projects totaling roughly 18,900 units have come online, down 19% from the same period last year.The Dallas-Fort Worth construction pipeline fell 7% year over year to roughly 42,200 units, driven mostly by a 20% drop in Fort Worth. Construction is concentrated in Frisco and Allen/McKinney, which hold about 30% of units underway.Multifamily permitting activity slowed through the third quarter of 2026. Developers pulled permits for roughly 16,700 units year to date, down 11% from the same period last year.Forecast: Multifamily permitting is projected to end 2026 at roughly 22,000 units, slightly below 2025 levels. Deliveries are expected to total about 25,000 units, a decline of more than 20% that would bring completions closer to long-term trends.Vacancy:Year-to-date demand outpaced new supply. Image The Dallas-Fort Worth vacancy rate edged down 10 basis points during the third quarter to 6.0%, extending the second quarter’s improvement and bringing the annual decline to 20 basis points. Performance diverged across the Metroplex, as vacancy declined 20 basis points during the quarter to 5.9% in Dallas but edged up 10 basis points to 6.4% in Fort Worth.Net absorption totaled approximately 26,100 units through the third quarter, nearly matching last year’s pace, but with deliveries down almost 20%, demand outpaced new supply by roughly 7,700 units, double the margin of a year ago.Occupancy gains shifted toward the lower end of the quality spectrum during the third quarter. Class C vacancy declined 30 basis points to 6.8%, the largest improvement among the classes, while Class A vacancy edged down 10 basis points to 5.2% and remained the tightest among the classes.Forecast: Vacancy is expected to moderate slightly during the fourth quarter as supply and demand return closer to equilibrium. Even so, the rate is still projected to end 2026 at 6.2%, 70 basis points below the year-end 2025 level.Rents:Annual rent growth in the Metroplex turned positive. items.title: Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?
items.description: Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates ? 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%. Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed's hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there? 1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable. 2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war. 3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently. We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads' job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.96% today, not 7.33% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.26% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. We saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 53,490 2025: 58,612 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 17 positive week-to-week prints 25 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 17 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time. Atlanta multifamily market overviewAtlanta’s multifamily market continued to improve in the third quarter of 2026, as asking rents edged higher and vacancy declined. Deliveries increased for a second consecutive quarter, rising 15% from the prior three months to about 3,100 units completed. Even so, completions remained 23% below the year-earlier level, and year-to-date deliveries are down 42% from the same period of 2025. The construction pipeline contracted to roughly 18,200 units underway, down 11% from the prior quarter. New deliveries spanned multiple submarkets, led by Northeast Gwinnett County and Buckhead. Buckhead also recorded the strongest absorption, followed by Northeast Gwinnett County and Kennesaw/Acworth. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% YOY decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 psf, a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. NYC Capital Markets: Volume Moderates but Remains on Track for Recovery Year After four quarters of sustained recovery, investment sales slowed in the third quarter. Dollar volume totaled $5.6 billion, a 30.7% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) decline and the first quarter since Q2 2025 to fall short of at least $8.0 billion. Investor confidence, which had steadily improved over the last year, was tempered by rising interest rates, uncertainty around the broader economy and geopolitical conditions, and the historically consistent trend of an election cycle pause. Despite the slowdown, the year-to-date (YTD) dollar volume total of $22.0 billion remains virtually unchanged from the same period last year, while the year’s annualized pace of $29.3 billion would represent a 23.3% increase over the 2020 cyclical low. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% year-over-year (YOY) decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 per square foot (psf), a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Sector Highlights Office: Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. Although activity remains muted compared to historical levels, the investor pool is steadily expanding, with deals this quarter completed by a diverse mix of institutional, REIT, private capital, and user-purchasers. The average deal size declined for the third consecutive quarter, to $46.8 million, as smaller private capital players deployed more capital into value-add strategies for discounted and underutilized assets. At the same time, larger investors remain attracted to well-positioned, sizeable Class A assets with favorable tenancy and capital improvement conditions. Pricing has declined nominally this year, down 4.2% to $478 psf. Multifamily: Although combined dollar volume for elevator and walk-up properties slowed to $1.1 billion in Q3 2026, the YTD total of $4.8 billion falls only 11.7% short of the total from the same period last year, which marked the strongest year since 2022. Similar to the office sector, multifamily demand is starkly bifurcated between market-rate, newly-constructed, often luxury assets versus majority-rent-regulated, deeply discounted offerings—though both segments are exhibiting encouraging momentum. Substantial renter demand has kept vacancy at historic lows and attracted a growing pool of capital from both core/core-plus investors as well as value-add players. Development: Volume pulled back slightly to $831.6 million in Q3 2026, but the sector remains on pace to finish at $5.0 billion: if achieved, 2026 and 2025 would be the only two years since 2019 to surpass that benchmark. Depressed land values and a still-limited supply pipeline continued to drive activity. That momentum, previously focused in Manhattan, has begun to spread to the city’s secondary markets: four out of the five largest development transactions this quarter were located in the Outer Boroughs, totaling $249.6 million across 1.3 million buildable square feet. Increased demand has continued to support pricing recovery, with the citywide price per buildable square foot rising 6.4% YOY to $227, the highest average since 2019. items.title: Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline
items.description: While October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low. National housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000. Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum. "Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units," according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where new home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023. Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million. “Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming said in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.” The new data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400. Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline. “Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he said. Homes under construction slip as completions lag The stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023. Meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025. Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year. Regional trends Year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers. The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely. Zillow Senior Economist Kenny Lee noted that the slowdown in single-family starts and permits indicates that homebuilders may be preparing for a relatively weak spring selling season. “While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane,” Lee explained. items.title: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage
items.description: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage New Zillow analysis finds that in October 2026, buyers in the highest credit band got a mortgage rate 36 basis points lower than buyers in the lowest band Written by Kara Ng on November 17, 2026 Key findings In October 2026, buyers with a credit score of 740 or higher were quoted a 7.23% rate on average on a 30-year fixed mortgage. Those with a credit score between 680 and 739 typically were quoted a 7.45% rate, while those with a score below 680 on average were quoted a rate of 7.59%, a 36-basis-point spread between the highest and lowest credit bands. With a 20% down payment, the total monthly payment on a typical U.S. home in October, worth $364,812, would have been $2,656 in the lowest credit score band and $2,584 in the highest. That’s an annual savings of $864 for those with the best credit scores. As of October 2026, a median-income household with a score of 740 or higher could afford a $317,572 home, versus $308,924 for a score below 680. That gap puts about 21,500 more active listings within reach nationwide. A higher credit score can be worth real money. A buyer with a strong credit score (740 or higher) can save more than $800 per year compared to a buyer with a low credit score (300-679) when buying the typical U.S. home. Those savings would have brought about 21,500 additional listings within budget nationwide for a median-income household in October. A better credit score changes the affordability math Home buyers with higher credit scores often receive a lower mortgage rate on their loan, which means a lower monthly payment. In October, the average mortgage rate offered to buyers with strong credit scores was 7.23%, while buyers with low credit scores were quoted a 7.59% rate, on average. For a typical U.S. home ($364,812) with a 20% down payment, that would mean a difference of $72 in each month’s mortgage payment, or $864 a year. Buyers with good scores of 680 to 739 sat in between, with a 7.45% rate, on average. That means they would pay $348 a year less than someone with a low credit score, but $516 a year more than someone with a strong credit score. These savings stretch a home buyer's budget, bringing more homes within reach. In October, a median-income household with a low credit score could afford a $308,924 home — meaning it would spend no more than 30% of its income on housing costs — given the average mortgage rate on offer. If that same median-income household had a strong credit score, it could afford a $317,572 home, an increase of about $8,650 in buying power. Where a better score is worth the most A better credit score brings the biggest potential savings in coastal markets, where home values are higher. Across the 50 largest metro areas, moving from a low credit score to a strong one saves anywhere from $45 a month in Pittsburgh to $304 in San Jose. A home buyer in San Jose could save $3,648 a year by moving from a low credit score to a strong one, followed by San Francisco ($2,688), Los Angeles ($2,256), San Diego ($2,208) and New York ($1,740). San Jose buyers would also enjoy the largest gain in buying power from improving their credit score at $18,778, ahead of Seattle ($14,896), San Francisco ($14,602), Raleigh ($13,688) and Washington, D.C. ($13,489). The smallest annual savings are in Pittsburgh ($540), Oklahoma City ($576), Memphis ($576) and Cleveland ($588). These are markets where mortgage payments are relatively inexpensive already, so there is less room for improvement with a lower rate. October's rate gap was the narrowest of 2026 The 36-basis-point spread in mortgage rates offered to buyers with strong and low credit scores in October was the narrowest of the year. Across the first 10 months of 2026, the rate difference between the lowest and highest credit bands ranged from 36 basis points in October to 58 basis points in April, with a median of 46 basis points. The monthly payment gap ranged from $72 in October to $110 in April, with a median of about $88, so the typical buyer in the lowest band paid roughly $1,050 a year more than a buyer in the highest band over that stretch. Improving their credit score is not the only way a buyer can secure a better rate. Buyers can also compare offers from multiple lenders , yet few actually do. Among buyers who contacted a lender, 62% contacted only one, according to Zillow's 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . Methodology Rates come from Zillow's Custom Quotes marketplace and reflect 30-year fixed conventional conforming purchase loans with 20% down or more. Credit bands are 300-679, 680-739 and 740+, and rates are quoted nationally. Quotes do not come from Zillow Home Loans. Data is as of October 2026. Affordability is calculated for a median-income household in a given region. Monthly payment is the total estimated payment for a typical home in a given region with 20% down, including estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. items.title: New Home Lot Supply Index
items.description: New Home Lot Supply Index The New Home Lot Supply Index provides an unrivaled look into the lot markets across the country, offering a current quarter snapshot as well as insight into the directional trend. This report details data for the third quarter of 2026. November 18, 2026 – 4 min read Table of Content: Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index (LSI) for 3Q26, rose for the ninth consecutive quarter and showed lot supply loosened both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter across the United States. The index is a residential real estate indicator based on the number of single-family vacant developed lots (VDL) and the rate at which those lots are absorbed via housing starts. The New Home LSI came in at 88.5 for 3Q26, representing a 20.8% increase from 3Q25. This quarter, the market continued to be rated “appropriately supplied.” On a quarter-over-quarter basis, supply increased by 3.9% from 2Q26. The LSI counts the total vacant developed lot supply and adjusts it for overall starts activity. “The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” said Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market. Affordability pressures and widespread incentives underscore the challenges builders face in converting demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market means availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction; it does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost challenges have disappeared.” In 2Q26, the LSI sat right on the boundary between "slightly undersupplied" and "appropriately supplied." However, the upward movement in Q3 solidified the national rating as “appropriately supplied.” In 3Q26, lot supply loosened year-over-year across all major metropolitan areas Zonda tracks, except Boise. For markets that saw an increase in lot supply, the average year-over-year gain was significant at +32%. More markets trended up and were rated “appropriately supplied” or “oversupplied” in the third quarter, but 12 out of 30 were still categorized as “significantly undersupplied.” The markets where land supply loosened the most on a year-over-year basis were Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle. Boise was the only market where local lot supply tightened compared to 3Q25, falling from 65.7 to 51.9, joining one of 12 markets rated “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed ratings this quarter, as outlined in the chart below: Zonda also records future lots through the stages of development. The stages range from raw land through streets in, which is the last step before the lot becomes a vacant developed lot. Zonda groups the last few stages into a classification called total upcoming lots, which typically indicates delivery over the next 12-18 months. Total upcoming lots in 3Q26 increased 1.0% year-over-year and 1.6% quarter-over-quarter. These types of lots in the third quarter were down 12.2% from the 2022 peak but were up 23.4% compared to the same quarter in 2019. Among total upcoming lots, roadwork was down 15.3% year-over-year. Roadwork is comprised of the two smaller stages—streets paved and streets in—and represents the last step in lot development. Lots in the excavation stage were up 8.6% year-over-year, and those with equipment on site were up 5.7%. The largest share of total upcoming lots were in the excavation stage in 3Q26, totaling 416K. These lots have an expected delivery between 2Q27 and 3Q27 (the range represents different timeframes from local entitlement processes). Note, not all of the lots in excavation will match Zonda’s estimated timeline. “The development pipeline is edging higher, but the mix of activity matters,” Fergus said. “More lots are in excavation and equipment-on-site stages than a year ago, while fewer are in the final roadwork stages. That points to continued investment in future communities, but an uneven flow of near-term deliveries. Builders will need to weigh today’s softer demand environment against the time required to prepare lots for future construction.” Get a first look at Land AI Get a first look at Zonda Land AI on December 10th. items.title: Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?
items.description: AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives? The Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that's not what's happening. I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline. Oil prices Oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off . Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t. In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk ) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money. In any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we announced a deal with Iran in June. AI stocks I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing issues, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced. The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune. Fed went into hawkish overdrive If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama. 10-year yield bounced off key support line For the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let's take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren't lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks. Conclusion The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates . Related More:

Lester November 13, 2026 Seeking a more suburban lifestyle—with the additional space, yard, and private garage often found in a single-family home—does not necessarily require stretching the budget to buy. For most families, buying is a significant financial stretch. A household that can comfortably afford rent on a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay increase to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before setting aside money for a down payment. Across the country, the typical rent for a single-family home is $2,243 per month, compared with $2,603 per month to own one with a 20% down payment—a difference of $360 each month. Using the common guideline of spending no more than 30% of household income on housing, a household needs to earn $89,724 to comfortably afford rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a deliberate choice, not a fallback. It requires less income than ownership and leaves more room in the monthly budget. The income increase required to buy a home is now the largest since early 2025, exceeding twice the $6,463 needed in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly dipped below 6%. The difference varies considerably by market. It is greatest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than twice the income needed to rent ($190,561)—a gap of $214,364. San Francisco has the next-largest gap at $139,353, followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual differences are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require an income increase. Even after securing that increase, prospective buyers face another challenge: saving for a 20% down payment. According to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report, about 30% of mortgage buyers receive a gift or loan from family or friends, while 46% rely on at least two sources, including down payment assistance programs. Beyond monthly expenses, households weighing renting against buying should consider purchase-related upfront costs, the potential to build equity and renters’ option to invest the money they would otherwise use for a down payment. Zillow’s rent-versus-buy analysis estimates the national break-even point—the time an owner must stay in a home for buying to become more advantageous than renting—at 7.8 years with a 20% down payment. items.title: Everyday Economics: The federal government delayed the housing recovery – The Center Square
items.description: Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Houses line a suburban neighborhood. Photo: Alan Wooten / The Center Square Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (The Center Square) – Existing-home sales fell in October to their slowest pace since August 2010, according to the National Association of Realtors . Federal policy is pulling in two directions: HUD has cut lenders’ costs on taxpayer-backed FHA loans, while tariffs, the conflict with Iran and federal borrowing add to the inflation and interest-rate pressures that keep mortgages expensive. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed rate has been climbing since the war began and now exceeds year ago levels. According to the National Association of Realtors , October existing-home sales fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the weakest pace since August 2010, and 8.8% below a year earlier. According to my calculations using NAR’s unadjusted data , actual October closings fell 11.7%, partly because October had one fewer business day than last year. The unadjusted annual decline deepened sharply from September’s 4.2%. The year started better than those figures suggest. According to the same calculations, 3.4 million homes sold through October, just 0.6% fewer than during the same period in 2025. My October housing report , based on Redfin data, found that seasonally adjusted pending sales fell 3.6% from September to their lowest level since April 2020. The same report found that active listings increased even though fewer sellers listed, because homes are selling more slowly. The problem is still affordability. My report calculated that monthly principal and interest on the median-priced home reached $2,137 with 20% down, up 11.2% from a year earlier. By my calculation, higher rates added approximately $223 to the monthly payment, while a slightly lower Redfin median sale price saved about $7. HUD has targeted a different cost: making the loan. According to HUD , June changes streamlined FHA appraisal-review requirements and eliminated a duplicative homebuyer disclosure form. HUD estimates the appraisal change alone saves lenders about $425 per review, or roughly $3.3 million a year industrywide. HUD’s announcement does not say how much of those savings will reach borrowers. The Appraisal Institute has said eliminating long-standing review requirements raises questions about oversight of collateral on FHA loans, which the federal government insures, American Banker reported . Any savings from lower origination costs are expected to be small next to the roughly $223 a month that higher rates added to the typical payment. Other federal policies affect what borrowers pay each month. According to Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers , tariffs raise prices for imported and domestically produced goods. According to the Energy Information Administration , attacks on tankers, constrained shipping and falling inventories pushed oil prices higher again in October. Federal borrowing matters, too. According to the Congressional Budget Office , growing government debt crowds out private investment and contributes to higher interest rates. My analysis found that sticky inflation and worries about U.S. fiscal sustainability have pushed long-term Treasury yields higher, and mortgage rates track those long-term yields far more closely than the Federal Reserve’s policy rate. Producer prices are still rising. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), producer prices rose 6.5% over the year through October, their largest increase since November 2022. BLS reported that truck freight prices rose 3.9% in October, accounting for more than 80% of the increase in services prices, even as diesel prices fell 7.9% from September. Truck freight prices were up 24.6% from a year earlier, according to BLS. According to my analysis of BLS producer price data, retail margins narrowed for computers, appliances and sporting goods, consistent with shoppers resisting higher prices. This week’s retail sales report could help clarify how spending is holding up. Retail sales and builder confidence arrive Tuesday, followed by housing starts and permits Wednesday. Orphe Divounguy, PhD, is chief economist for The Center Square and founder and chief economist of Quantitative Research Group, the co-host of the Everyday Economics podcast and a former economist at Zillow. He has briefed the White House Council of Economic Advisers, testified before state legislatures, and delivers more than 30 speaking engagements annually. Orphe also has a large media footprint, typically 300-400 media mentions per quarter. He specializes in housing, labor markets, and the broader economy. items.title: South Atlantic Apartment Supply Set to Rebound in 2027
items.description: South Atlantic Apartment Supply Set to Rebound in 2027 by Carl Whitaker Posted November 9, 2026 in Insights While supply pressure eases across much of the Sun Belt, the South Atlantic is heading the other way, with 2027 apartment deliveries forecast to climb above 2026 levels. After a pullback in 2026, new apartment supply across Delaware, DC, Maryland, North Carolina and Virginia is forecast to rise to over 41,900 units in 2027. That is an increase of more than 11,400 units, or roughly 38%, and a notable contrast with several Sun Belt peers, where lighter construction is translating into a thinner delivery pipeline. The increase is not evenly spread. Charlotte (up 5,186 units to 13,543) and Raleigh/Durham (up 4,186 to 9,441) account for more than 80% of the regional jump, while Richmond, Washington, DC and Greensboro also see more deliveries. Carolina markets enter 2027 with strong demand foundations, but more than one-third of Charlotte units are already offering concessions. The 2027 wave is also more concentrated in select submarkets than the metro-wide surge of 2023 and 2024, and total deliveries remain well below the 2024 peak of roughly 65,600 units. Even so, it will take a strong year of demand to absorb this much new supply. East Bay Oakland vacancy increased the most year-over-year, up 230 bps or 255,104 square feet (sf) from the same quarter last year, largely due to the delivery of new construction projects that completed in 2025. Additional consolidations also contributed to vacancy over the last 18 months. items.title: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak
items.description: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak by Kim O'Brien Posted November 5, 2026 in Insights San Diego apartment supply hit a record high in the past year and is set to peak in 1st quarter 2027. In the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, roughly 6,600 units completed across San Diego, marking the highest annual total since Realpage Market Analytics began tracking the market in 2000. Supply in the past year also surpassed the market’s decade average around the 4,000-unit mark. Annual supply in San Diego is expected to remain elevated, peaking in the year-ending 1st quarter 2027, when roughly 6,880 units are scheduled for completion. After that, supply is slated to come down, aligning closer to the market’s decade average by the end of 2027. Demand is keeping pace with record apartment supply in San Diego, as evidenced by occupancy at 95.7% in October and rents up 1.5% year-over-year. After supply hits its peak and starts to come down, this market is projected to see improvement in both of those metrics. items.title: Rates Jump Again as Inflation and War Worries Persist
items.description: Rates Jump Again as Inflation and War Worries Persist By Anthony Smith Nov 19, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate jumped 17 basis points to 7.28% this week, reversing four weeks of declines that had brought rates down to 7.11%, as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back toward 5%. Hot inflation data and the persistence of the conflict in Iran placed upward pressure on bond yields and borrowing costs. The October CPI report came in above expectations on both the headline and core measures, cementing market expectations for a December rate hike and giving the 10-year little room to fall. The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves. That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October , and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010 , as the surge in rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers alike. Builder confidence has also fallen to a 14-year low, and permit activity dropped to its lowest level since the early days of the pandemic , signaling that the supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? For buyers who remain active, conditions offer some real advantages. With fewer shoppers in the market, competition has thinned, sellers have shown more flexibility on price, and active inventory continues to rise even as new listings have pulled back. The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market.

items.title: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023
items.description: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023 By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Nov 18, 2026 Highlights October 2026 marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023. The change was modest with the median asking rent rising by just $1 (+0.1%) from October 2025 to $1,692. Rents continue to split the difference between their recent highs and prepandemic level. They are down $82 (-4.6%) from summer 2022 peak, and up $221 (+15%) from pre-pandemic level. Rent rebounded in larger units, while studio rents continue to soften: Studio: $1,411, down $17 (-1.2%) YoY 1-bed: $1,566, up $1(+0.1%) YoY 2-bed: $1,889, up $5 (+0.3%) YoY In 2026Q3, multifamily deliveries have returned to pre-pandemic levels as the 2021–2022 boom cohorts clear. Looking ahead, a cooling in starts suggests that new rental supply is likely to stay modest in the near term. Completions: 330,000, down 26% YoY Under Construction: 674,000, down 2.7% YoY Starts: 403,000, down 9.2% YoY All U.S. regions share the national pattern of cooling completions but differ in what comes next based on starts and the under-construction pipeline: the Northeast is rebuilding, the Midwest and South are easing from elevated levels, and the West looks the most likely to tighten. In October 2026, the median asking rent rose 0.1% year over year, the first annual increase since June 2023. Median asking rent for 0–2 bedroom properties across the 50 largest metro areas was $1,692, about $221 (15%) above the pre-pandemic level but $82 (-4.6%) below the August 2022 peak. Median asking rents fell year over year for more than three years, and the 2021–2022 multifamily construction boom was the main driver of the decline. Projects started in those years were delivered in 2023–2025 and added supply that held rents down. According to the Housing Vacancy Survey, the rental vacancy rate reached 7.6% in 2026Q3, the highest level since early 2014. However, as construction activity unwinds, the downward pressure on rents from new supply has eased. At the same time, elevated borrowing costs may be supporting rental demand by keeping more households renting. The path ahead largely depends on whether new multifamily deliveries remain strong enough to outpace that demand. Larger units see rents increase In October 2026, the median asking rent for two-bedroom units rose 0.3% year over year, the first annual increase since May 2023. At $1,889, the national median for two-bedroom units is $82 (4.2%) below its July 2022 peak. Even after more than three years of softness, it remains $299 (18.8%) above its level seven years ago. The rent for one-bedroom units increased 0.1% in October 2026 on a year over year basis, and now stands at $1,566. This was the first month of annual rent growth since June 2023. Rent was $95 (-5.7%) lower than the peak observed during August 2022, but still $191 (13.9%) higher than in October 2019. In October 2026, the median asking rent for studios fell by 1.2%, marking the 39th consecutive month of annual declines. The median rent of studios was $1,411 in October, down by $73 (-4.9%) from its peak, seen in Fall 2022. Nevertheless, the median asking rent for studios was still $141 (11.1%) higher than seven years ago.
